title: Stacking & Blending

blocks.t: From the notes
Stacking, as written

Stacking — we use different different algorithms as base
models, and then their predictions become the input for another model
called the meta model.

Base models are trained on the training data; the meta model is trained on the
predictions of the base models.

Blending — same idea but instead of K-fold, we keep a
holdout set aside for the meta model.

Bagging and boosting both build an ensemble out of one kind of learner
and combine it with a fixed rule (average, or weighted sum). Stacking
drops both restrictions.

The base models can be anything — logistic regression, KNN, a random forest,
an SVM, naive Bayes. And the combination rule is not fixed: it is
learned. The meta-model looks at a row of predictions
$(\hat p_{\text{logreg}}, \hat p_{\text{knn}}, \hat p_{\text{rf}},\dots)$ and
learns things like "when the forest and the SVM disagree, trust the forest",
or "naive Bayes is always overconfident, shrink it". That is strictly more
expressive than a plain average.
The leakage problem and why K-fold is mandatory

The single mistake that ruins stacking. If you train a base model on
the training set and then ask it to predict that same training set, its
predictions are far too good — a random forest will be near-perfect on rows it
memorised. The meta-model then learns "the forest is always right", because on
its training data it was. At test time the forest is merely good, the
meta-model's weights are wrong, and the stack underperforms a simple average.

blocks.cap:
Left: stacking. Each fold's model predicts only the fold it never saw,
so every training row receives an honest, out-of-fold prediction and the
meta-model can use all of them. Right: blending. One holdout split, simpler and
cheaper, but the meta-model sees far fewer rows.

blocks.t:
Let $\mathcal{D}=\{(x_i,y_i)\}_{i=1}^n$ and let $\kappa(i)\in\{1..K\}$ be the
fold of row $i$. For base learner $m$ let $f_m^{(-k)}$ be that learner trained
on all folds except $k$. The out-of-fold (OOF) matrix is

Z \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times M},
\qquad
Z_{im} = f_m^{(-\kappa(i))}(x_i).

Every entry is produced by a model that never saw row $i$, so $Z$ has the same
statistical character as predictions on unseen data. The meta-model $g$ is
fitted on $(Z, y)$.
At prediction time we need a $Z$ for the test rows. Two valid conventions:

items:
Refit each $f_m$ on the full training set and predict the test
set once (what sklearn does).

Average the folds: $\bar z_m(x)=\frac1K\sum_k f_m^{(-k)}(x)$
(common in competitions — slightly more stable, $K\times$ the inference cost).

blocks.cap:
Left: the leaky version reaches a near-perfect meta-training AUC
and a worse test AUC. Right: pairs of base models with lower prediction
correlation stack better, even when their individual accuracies are similar.

blocks.t: Why diversity beats individual accuracy

blocks.cap:
Measured on 4000 rows. Left: the stack beats every base model and the
plain average. Middle: correlation between OOF predictions — green is
uncorrelated, and the uncorrelated pairs are what the stack exploits. Right:
the learned meta-coefficients, including a negative one.

blocks.t:
Look at the middle panel. Logistic regression and the SVM agree almost
perfectly (both draw smooth global boundaries), so adding the second one buys
almost nothing. Naive Bayes is the worst single model but the least
correlated with the forest — and it earns a real meta-coefficient, because
where it is right, it is right for different reasons.

This mirrors the variance algebra from bagging: averaging $M$ estimators with
pairwise correlation $\rho$ gives variance
$\rho\sigma^2 + \frac{1-\rho}{M}\sigma^2$. As $\rho\to1$ the ensemble stops
helping. Stacking generalises this — it can even use a negative
coefficient, effectively subtracting a model's systematic bias, which plain
averaging can never do.
How to pick base models

Choose learners with different inductive biases, not different
hyperparameters of the same learner:

items: a tree ensemble (axis-aligned, captures interactions, cannot extrapolate),
a distance-based model, KNN or RBF SVM (local),
a probabilistic model, naive Bayes (different assumptions entirely),

blocks.t:
Five variants of a random forest will produce five near-identical columns and a
useless stack.
Choosing the meta-model

Keep the meta-model simple. It has $M$ features (a handful) and
$n$ rows, but those features are highly correlated with each other and with the
target — exactly the setting where a flexible model overfits. Regularised
logistic or linear regression is the standard choice; RidgeCV for
regression, LogisticRegression for classification.

Non-negative least squares is another good option: it forces the combination to
be a weighted average, which is more stable and interpretable, at the cost of
losing the bias-cancelling negative weights.

A gradient-boosted meta-model occasionally helps when you also feed the original
features to level 2 (passthrough=True in sklearn), letting the
meta-learner condition on where in feature space it is before deciding
whom to trust. Use it with care — it is a large jump in capacity.
Stacking vs blending

head: Stacking (K-fold OOF)
Blending (holdout)
rows: data is huge, time is short, or folds are unsafe (time series, grouped data)

blocks.t:
Nested leakage. If you tune base-model hyperparameters using the same
CV folds you later use to generate OOF predictions, the OOF matrix is
optimistically biased and the stack's validation score lies. Tune inside an
inner loop, or tune on a separate split, or accept that your reported number is
slightly optimistic and confirm on a truly untouched test set.

Grouped / temporal data. Random K-fold will put the same customer, or a
future time period, on both sides of a fold boundary. Use GroupKFold or
TimeSeriesSplit to build the OOF matrix, otherwise every level of the
stack inherits the leak.
Code

import numpy as np
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
from sklearn.model_selection import (train_test_split, StratifiedKFold,
                                     cross_val_predict, cross_val_score)
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression, RidgeCV
from sklearn.ensemble import (RandomForestClassifier, StackingClassifier,
                              StackingRegressor, GradientBoostingClassifier)
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier
from sklearn.svm import SVC
from sklearn.naive_bayes import GaussianNB
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score

X, y = make_classification(n_samples=4000, n_features=25, n_informative=12,
                           n_redundant=5, flip_y=0.04, random_state=0)
Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.3,
                                      stratify=y, random_state=0)

# ==================================================================
# 1. STACKING BY HAND -- so the OOF matrix is not a black box
# ==================================================================
base = [
    ("logreg", make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000))),
    ("knn"   , make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), KNeighborsClassifier(25))),
    ("rf"    , RandomForestClassifier(300, random_state=0, n_jobs=4)),
    ("svc"   , make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), SVC(probability=True, random_state=0))),
    ("nb"    , GaussianNB()),
]

cv = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=0)
n, M = len(ytr), len(base)

Z_train = np.zeros((n, M))            # the out-of-fold matrix
Z_test  = np.zeros((len(yte), M))

for j, (name, model) in enumerate(base):
    # cross_val_predict gives EXACTLY the OOF predictions: each row is
    # predicted by the fold-model that did not train on it.
    Z_train[:, j] = cross_val_predict(model, Xtr, ytr, cv=cv,
                                      method="predict_proba", n_jobs=4)[:, 1]
    # refit on the FULL training set for the test-time column
    model.fit(Xtr, ytr)
    Z_test[:, j] = model.predict_proba(Xte)[:, 1]
    print(f"{name:7s} solo AUC {roc_auc_score(yte, Z_test[:, j]):.4f}")

meta = LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000).fit(Z_train, ytr)
print("STACK   AUC", round(roc_auc_score(yte, meta.predict_proba(Z_test)[:, 1]), 4))
print("mean    AUC", round(roc_auc_score(yte, Z_test.mean(axis=1)), 4))
print("meta weights:", dict(zip([n_ for n_, _ in base], meta.coef_[0].round(3))))

# Diversity check -- this table tells you which members are earning their keep
print(np.corrcoef(Z_train.T).round(2))

# ==================================================================
# 2. THE LEAKY VERSION -- what NOT to do
# ==================================================================
Z_leak = np.zeros((n, M))
for j, (_, model) in enumerate(base):
    model.fit(Xtr, ytr)
    Z_leak[:, j] = model.predict_proba(Xtr)[:, 1]   # <-- IN-SAMPLE. WRONG.
meta_leak = LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000).fit(Z_leak, ytr)
print("leaky  meta-train AUC",
      round(roc_auc_score(ytr, meta_leak.predict_proba(Z_leak)[:, 1]), 4))  # ~1.0
print("leaky  test       AUC",
      round(roc_auc_score(yte, meta_leak.predict_proba(Z_test)[:, 1]), 4))  # worse

# ==================================================================
# 3. THE SKLEARN WAY -- StackingClassifier does all of the above
# ==================================================================
stack = StackingClassifier(
        estimators      = base,
        final_estimator = LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000),
        cv              = cv,        # how the OOF matrix is built
        stack_method    = "predict_proba",
        passthrough     = False,     # True -> also give the meta the raw X
        n_jobs          = 4)
stack.fit(Xtr, ytr)
print("sklearn stack AUC",
      round(roc_auc_score(yte, stack.predict_proba(Xte)[:, 1]), 4))

# Honest evaluation: cross-validate the WHOLE stack, not just the meta-model.
print("nested CV AUC:",
      cross_val_score(stack, X, y, cv=3, scoring="roc_auc", n_jobs=1).round(4))

# ==================================================================
# 4. BLENDING -- one holdout, no folds
# ==================================================================
Xa, Xhold, ya, yhold = train_test_split(Xtr, ytr, test_size=0.2,
                                        stratify=ytr, random_state=0)
H  = np.zeros((len(yhold), M))
T  = np.zeros((len(yte),   M))
for j, (_, model) in enumerate(base):
    model.fit(Xa, ya)                       # base models see 80% only
    H[:, j] = model.predict_proba(Xhold)[:, 1]
    T[:, j] = model.predict_proba(Xte)[:, 1]
blender = LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000).fit(H, yhold)
print("BLEND   AUC", round(roc_auc_score(yte, blender.predict_proba(T)[:, 1]), 4))

# ==================================================================
# 5. REGRESSION + MULTI-LEVEL + SAFE FOLDS
# ==================================================================
from sklearn.datasets import make_regression
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestRegressor
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
Xr, yr = make_regression(n_samples=3000, n_features=20, noise=15, random_state=0)
sreg = StackingRegressor(
        estimators=[("lin", LinearRegression()),
                    ("rf" , RandomForestRegressor(200, random_state=0, n_jobs=4))],
        final_estimator=RidgeCV(alphas=np.logspace(-3, 3, 13)),
        cv=5, n_jobs=4).fit(Xr[:2000], yr[:2000])
print("stacked R2:", round(sreg.score(Xr[2000:], yr[2000:]), 4))

# Level-2 stacks are just stacks whose members are stacks:
level2 = StackingClassifier(
        estimators=[("stack1", stack),
                    ("gb", GradientBoostingClassifier(random_state=0))],
        final_estimator=LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000), cv=3, n_jobs=1)
# (expensive -- rarely worth more than 2 levels outside competitions)

# Grouped or temporal data: swap the fold generator, everything else is the same
from sklearn.model_selection import GroupKFold, TimeSeriesSplit
# StackingClassifier(..., cv=GroupKFold(5))   # needs groups= passed to fit
# StackingClassifier(..., cv=TimeSeriesSplit(5))
Everything on one page
Summary

Stacking learns the combination rule. Base models of different
types produce predictions; a meta-model is trained on those predictions.

The OOF matrix is the whole trick. $Z_{im}=f_m^{(-\kappa(i))}(x_i)$ —
every entry from a model that never saw that row. Training the meta-model on
in-sample predictions is the classic failure and produces a stack worse than a
plain average.

Blending replaces K-fold with one holdout: cheaper and simpler, but the
meta-model trains on far fewer rows.

Diversity $>$ individual accuracy. A weak, uncorrelated model earns a
place; a strong, redundant one does not. Read the OOF correlation matrix before
adding members.

Keep level 2 simple — regularised linear. And evaluate the
whole pipeline with an outer CV, never the meta-model alone.

Cost: $M\times K$ base fits. Real gains are typically 0.5–2% —
decisive in a competition, often not worth the operational complexity in
production, where you must now train, version and serve $M+1$ models.
Interview corner
Q. How does stacking differ from bagging and boosting?

Bagging: one algorithm, parallel, combined by a fixed average, attacks
variance. Boosting: one algorithm, sequential, fixed weighted sum, attacks
bias. Stacking: several different algorithms, and the combination itself
is a learned model.
Q. Why must the meta-model be trained on out-of-fold predictions?

In-sample predictions are unrealistically accurate, especially for
high-variance learners. The meta-model would learn weights calibrated to that
fiction. OOF predictions have the same error profile as unseen data, so the
learned weights transfer.
Q. Stacking vs blending — when do you pick blending?

When data is plentiful (a 10% holdout is still tens of thousands of rows),
when compute is tight, or when K-fold would leak — time series or grouped
data where a naive fold split puts related rows on both sides.
Q. How do you choose base models?

By inductive-bias diversity: linear, tree ensemble, distance-based,
probabilistic. Check the OOF correlation matrix — members correlated above
about 0.95 are redundant. A weaker but decorrelated model often contributes
more than a stronger duplicate.
Q. Can a stack be worse than its best base model?

Yes — from leakage in the OOF construction, from an overfit meta-model (too
flexible, or too few meta rows in blending), or from redundant members that
make the meta-features collinear. Always compare against both the best single
model and a plain average.
Q. What does passthrough=True do?

It gives the meta-model the original features alongside the base predictions,
so it can learn region-dependent trust ("in this part of feature space, prefer
the forest"). More expressive, more overfitting risk; needs a regularised or
tree-based meta-model and more data.
Q. Why can a meta-coefficient be negative?

Because the meta-model is doing regression, not averaging. If a model has a
systematic bias correlated with another member's error, subtracting it removes
that error. This is expressive power a simple average does not have — and one
reason a stack can beat every member.
Worked Examples
How stacking and blending build the meta-training set
Three base models $M_1,M_2,M_3$, $n = 1000$ training rows.
Stacking with $K=4$ folds.

items: Split the 1000 rows into 4 folds of 250.
Train $M_1$ on 3 folds (750 rows), predict the held-out fold (250 rows). Repeat for each fold. Every row now gets exactly one out-of-fold prediction from $M_1$.
Do the same for $M_2$ and $M_3$. The meta-training matrix is $1000\times 3$: each row carries three out-of-fold predictions, and no row was predicted by a model that trained on it.
Train the meta-model on this matrix. For test data, average the test predictions of each base model's fold copies (or retrain each base on all 1000 rows).

blocks.t: Blending with a hold-out.

items: Train each base model on the 800 rows, predict the 200 blend rows.

blocks.t: Trade-off. Stacking uses all 1000 rows for the meta-model but costs $K$ times more base-model fits. Blending is cheaper, but the meta-model learns from only 200 rows, so it is noisier. The leakage the chapter warns about is the case where a base model's training rows also appear in the meta-training matrix; both schemes prevent it.
